questions.text: What is the type of the value produced by `3 / 2` in Python 3?
questions.explanation: The / operator always performs true division and returns a float, so 3 / 2 is 1.5.

questions.text: Which keyword is used to define a named function in Python?
questions.explanation: Named functions are created with def. The lambda keyword creates anonymous functions.

questions.text: What does `len("Python")` return?
questions.explanation: The string Python contains six characters, so len returns 6.

questions.text: Which of these built-in types is immutable?
questions.explanation: Tuples cannot be changed after creation. Lists, dictionaries and sets are mutable.

questions.text: What is the value of `bool([])`?
questions.explanation: Empty containers are falsy in Python, so bool of an empty list is False.

questions.text: What does `"ab" * 3` evaluate to?
questions.explanation: Multiplying a string by an integer repeats it, giving ababab.

questions.text: Which sequence does `list(range(2, 10, 3))` produce?
questions.explanation: range starts at 2, steps by 3 and stops before 10, giving 2, 5 and 8.

questions.text: After `x = [1, 2, 3]`, `y = x` and `y.append(4)`, what does `print(x)` show?
questions.explanation: Assignment copies the reference, not the list, so x and y are the same object.

questions.text: What does `0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3` evaluate to in Python?
questions.explanation: Binary floating point cannot represent 0.1 and 0.2 exactly, so the sum is 0.30000000000000004.

questions.text: What is the behaviour of a default argument such as `def add(item, bucket=[])`?
options: The list is created once at definition time and shared across calls
A new list is created on every call
The list is reset after each call returns
questions.explanation: Default values are evaluated once when the function is defined, so a mutable default is shared between calls.

questions.text: What does `print(*[1, 2, 3], sep="-")` output?
questions.explanation: The star unpacks the list into separate arguments and sep joins them with a hyphen.

questions.text: What does the `nonlocal` keyword do?
options: Binds a name to a variable in the nearest enclosing function scope
Imports a name from another module
questions.explanation: nonlocal lets a nested function rebind a variable of an enclosing function instead of creating a new local.

questions.text: Which built-in Python type stores key-value pairs?
questions.explanation: A dict maps unique keys to values.

questions.text: Which list method adds one element to the end of the list?
questions.explanation: list.append(x) adds x at the end of the list.

questions.text: Which data structure follows last-in, first-out (LIFO) order?
questions.explanation: In a stack the most recently added element is removed first.

questions.text: Which built-in type does not allow duplicate elements?
questions.explanation: A set stores unique elements only.

questions.text: What is the average-case time complexity of looking up a key in a Python dict?
questions.explanation: Dictionaries are hash tables, so lookups take constant time on average.

questions.text: Which standard library class provides an efficient double-ended queue?
questions.explanation: collections.deque supports O(1) appends and pops at both ends.

questions.text: What does `{1, 2, 3} & {2, 3, 4}` evaluate to?
questions.explanation: The & operator on sets is intersection: elements present in both.

questions.text: Which traversal of a binary search tree visits the keys in ascending order?
questions.explanation: Inorder traversal visits left subtree, node, then right subtree, which yields sorted order for a BST.

questions.text: What is the worst-case time to search an unbalanced binary search tree with n nodes?
questions.explanation: If keys are inserted in sorted order the tree degenerates into a linked list, so a search may visit every node.

questions.text: Which standard library module implements a min-heap on top of a plain list?
questions.explanation: heapq provides heappush and heappop that maintain the heap invariant in a list.

questions.text: Why can a list not be used as a dictionary key?
options: Lists are too large to hash
Lists are mutable and therefore unhashable
questions.explanation: Dictionary keys must be hashable and stable. Mutable lists do not define a hash.

questions.text: In a hash table with chaining, all keys collide into one bucket. What is the lookup time?
questions.explanation: With every key in one chain, a lookup must scan the whole chain.

questions.text: Which special method initialises a new instance of a class?
questions.explanation: __init__ runs right after an instance is created and sets up its attributes.

questions.text: What does `self` represent inside an instance method?
options: The instance the method was called on
questions.explanation: Python passes the instance as the first argument, conventionally named self.

questions.text: How do you declare that class B inherits from class A?
questions.explanation: Base classes are listed in parentheses after the class name.

questions.text: What is encapsulation?
options: Converting an object to a string
Bundling data with the methods that use it and limiting direct access to internal state
questions.explanation: Encapsulation keeps an object's state behind a controlled interface.

questions.text: What does a single leading underscore, as in `_name`, indicate by convention?
options: The attribute is for internal use
The attribute is a static method
questions.explanation: A single underscore is a convention only; Python does not enforce it.

questions.text: Which decorator defines a method that receives the class instead of an instance?
questions.explanation: A classmethod receives the class as its first argument, conventionally cls.

questions.text: What is polymorphism?
options: Different classes offering the same interface so one call works on many types
questions.explanation: Polymorphism lets code call the same method on different types and get type-specific behaviour.

questions.text: What does `super().__init__()` do in a subclass initialiser?
questions.explanation: super() gives access to the next class in the method resolution order, here to run its __init__.

questions.text: In `class C(A, B)`, what determines the order in which base classes are searched for a method?
options: The order classes appear in the file
questions.explanation: Python computes the MRO using C3 linearisation; it can be inspected with C.__mro__.

questions.text: Which special method makes an instance callable like a function?
questions.explanation: Defining __call__ lets you write instance(...).

questions.text: What is the effect of defining `__slots__` in a class?
options: Instances are limited to the listed attributes and avoid a per-instance __dict__
questions.explanation: __slots__ fixes the attribute names and saves memory by not creating an instance dictionary.

questions.text: How does Python treat an attribute named `__secret` inside class `Account`?
questions.explanation: Name mangling rewrites the name to reduce accidental clashes; it is not real access control.

questions.text: Which Flask decorator registers a function as the handler for a URL?
questions.explanation: @app.route maps a URL rule to a view function.

questions.text: Which Flask function renders an HTML template?
questions.explanation: render_template loads a Jinja2 template and fills it with the given variables.

questions.text: Which HTTP method is normally used to submit a form that creates data?
questions.explanation: POST sends data in the request body and is meant for state-changing requests.

questions.text: Which template engine does Flask use by default?
questions.explanation: Flask ships with Jinja2 as its template engine.

questions.text: Which Flask object keeps per-user data across requests in a signed cookie?
questions.explanation: The session is stored client-side in a cookie signed with SECRET_KEY.

questions.text: What is the purpose of a CSRF token?
options: To ensure state-changing requests come from the site's own forms
questions.explanation: A secret per-session token that attackers cannot read stops other sites from forging requests.

questions.text: What is a Flask Blueprint used for?
options: Organising routes and related code into reusable modules
questions.explanation: Blueprints group routes, templates and static files so large apps stay modular.

questions.text: Which HTTP status code means the requested resource was not found?
questions.explanation: 404 Not Found indicates the server has no resource at that URL.

questions.text: Why store passwords with a slow, salted hash such as scrypt rather than plain SHA-256?
options: It allows the password to be decrypted later
It makes brute-force attacks costly and gives identical passwords different hashes
questions.explanation: A per-password salt and tunable cost make large-scale guessing expensive.

questions.text: What does the application factory pattern, `create_app()`, make possible?
options: Creating several app instances with different configurations, such as for testing
questions.explanation: A factory builds the app on demand, so tests and deployments can each use their own configuration.

questions.text: What does setting SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY to True prevent?
options: JavaScript in the page from reading the session cookie
The server from reading the cookie
The cookie being sent over HTTPS
questions.explanation: HttpOnly cookies are hidden from document.cookie, limiting damage from XSS.

questions.text: Why is Gunicorn used in production instead of `flask run`?
options: The built-in development server is not designed for production load or security
Gunicorn compiles Flask code to C
questions.explanation: Gunicorn is a production WSGI server with worker management, unlike the development server.

questions.text: What is the time complexity of binary search on a sorted array of n items?
questions.explanation: Each comparison halves the search range.

questions.text: Which sorting algorithm repeatedly swaps adjacent elements that are out of order?
questions.explanation: Bubble sort compares neighbouring items and swaps them until the list is sorted.

questions.text: What must every recursive function have to avoid infinite recursion?
questions.explanation: The base case stops the recursion.

questions.text: What is the time complexity of reading a list element by index?
questions.explanation: Lists are arrays, so indexing takes constant time.

questions.text: Which paradigm splits a problem into smaller subproblems, solves them and combines the results?
questions.explanation: Merge sort is the classic divide-and-conquer example.

questions.text: What is the worst-case time complexity of quicksort?
questions.explanation: Consistently poor pivot choices produce unbalanced partitions and quadratic time.

questions.text: Which data structure does breadth-first search use to hold nodes to visit?
questions.explanation: BFS visits nodes level by level using a first-in, first-out queue.

questions.text: What is memoization?
options: Converting recursion into a loop automatically
Caching results of function calls to avoid repeated work
questions.explanation: Memoization stores computed results keyed by arguments.

questions.text: What is the time complexity of merge sort in the best, average and worst cases?
questions.explanation: Merge sort always splits into halves and merges in linear time per level.

questions.text: Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm requires which condition on edge weights?
questions.explanation: Negative edges can invalidate the assumption that a finalised node's distance is optimal.

questions.text: How does dynamic programming differ from plain divide and conquer?
options: It works only on sorted data
It always runs in linear time
Subproblems overlap, so their results are stored and reused
questions.explanation: Overlapping subproblems are solved once and cached.

questions.text: What is the time complexity of `for i in range(n): for j in range(i): pass`?
questions.explanation: The inner loop runs 0+1+...+(n-1) = n(n-1)/2 times, which is quadratic.
